patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral foot numbness and tingling, worse at night, for 2.5 years
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Johnson is a 58-year-old African American woman with an 11-year history of type 2 diabetes who presents for evaluation of bilateral foot numbness and tingling that has been progressively worsening over the past 2.5 years. She describes the sensation as a constant tingling, like pins and needles, predominantly in her toes and the balls of her feet. More recently, she has developed a burning quality to the pain that is particularly bothersome at night, disrupting her sleep 3 to 4 times per week. The numbness has gradually extended from her toes to involve both feet entirely, and she now notes some numbness in the lower 6 inches of both legs. She reports difficulty feeling the texture of the ground while walking and has noted she cannot feel water temperature with her feet. Last month, she stepped on a small piece of glass and did not feel it until her daughter noticed blood on the floor. She has had recurrent small cuts and calluses on her feet that she only notices when bathing. She acknowledges her blood sugars have been inconsistently controlled, with home readings ranging widely from 80 to over 300 mg/dL. She has been compliant with her insulin and oral medications but admits dietary challenges. She denies upper extremity symptoms, weakness, or difficulty walking. She denies recent illness, new medications, or toxic exposures. Her hypothyroidism was diagnosed 4 years ago and she states her last TSH was within normal range per her primary care physician.

findings.nerve: EMG - right first dorsal interosseous foot

specialized_test.impression: Moderately severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy. Sural SNAPs are absent or markedly reduced bilaterally; superficial peroneal sensory is absent on the right. Lower extremity motor amplitudes are reduced with prolonged F-wave latency; upper extremity median and motor studies are preserved. No demyelinating features — no temporal dispersion, no conduction block, conduction velocities proportional to axonal loss. EMG demonstrates chronic denervation distally. Findings are consistent with a moderate-to-severe length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Severely reduced intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD) distally with a length-dependent gradient — distal leg 1.8 fibers/mm (reference >6.5) and proximal thigh 6.1 fibers/mm (reference >8.5). Findings confirm small fiber neuropathy with a distal-predominant gradient. Clinical correlation recommended.

quantitative_data.pattern: Distal sudomotor and cardiovagal autonomic neuropathy

output.impression: Moderate distal autonomic dysfunction — QSART absent at foot and markedly reduced at distal leg (0.15 uL/cm2; reference >0.3); cardiovagal studies show reduced heart rate variability (E:I ratio 1.06; Valsalva ratio 1.15, both below normal thresholds). Mild orthostatic hypotension confirmed on orthostatic testing (BP drop 18/8 mmHg at 2 min, symptomatic). Findings are consistent with predominantly distal sudomotor and cardiovagal autonomic neuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

critical_actions: Confirm diabetic neuropathy diagnosis with NCS/EMG
Check and replace vitamin B12 (metformin-induced deficiency)
Optimize glycemic control - HbA1c 9.6% too high
Start neuropathic pain medication (duloxetine preferred per ADA guidelines)

contraindicated_actions: Do not use tricyclic antidepressants as first-line in elderly diabetic with cardiovascular risk
Do not prescribe opioids for neuropathic pain without prior trial of first-line agents
Do not delay B12 replacement - ongoing metformin will continue to deplete B12
Do not attribute sensory loss to lumbar stenosis without NCS confirmation
key_reasoning_points: HbA1c 9.6% confirms poor glycemic control as the dominant driver of neuropathy
Low B12 (196 pg/mL) with elevated MMA (0.52 nmol/mL) confirms functional deficiency - a recognized metformin complication
NCS demonstrates classic axonal (not demyelinating) length-dependent pattern, distinguishing diabetic neuropathy from CIDP
Absent ankle reflexes and stocking-distribution sensory loss are hallmarks of length-dependent peripheral neuropathy
TSH is normal, excluding hypothyroid neuropathy as an alternative or contributing diagnosis
10-gram monofilament insensate at multiple plantar sites identifies high risk for diabetic foot ulceration
Duloxetine is FDA-approved for painful diabetic neuropathy and preferred per 2023 ADA Standards of Care
